prompt: `customers` has 568 pages. Its file is 4653056 bytes. How many bytes is one page?
hint: Divide, or remember block_size.

prompt: Why can a power cut leave a PostgreSQL page half new and half old on ext4?
hint: Compare the two units of writing.

choices.text: Its 8 kB spans two 4 kB filesystem blocks, written separately
choices.why: Right. One 8 kB page is two 4 kB blocks, and nothing makes both land together.

choices.text: PostgreSQL writes each row separately and stops halfway through the list of rows in a page
choices.why: PostgreSQL writes whole pages. The split happens below it, in the filesystem's smaller blocks.

choices.text: ext4 compresses pages and loses half on a crash
choices.why: ext4 does not compress data. The cause is the size mismatch, which any 4 kB filesystem has.

choices.text: The write-ahead log only records half of every page
choices.why: The opposite: after a checkpoint the log records the whole page, which is how a torn page is repaired.

prompt: A colleague wants to set `block_size = 4096` in postgresql.conf so pages match the filesystem. What happens?
hint: When is the page size decided?

choices.text: Torn pages stop happening after the next restart, because the page now matches the block
choices.why: The setting cannot be changed in a configuration file at all, so the restart changes nothing.

choices.text: Existing tables are rewritten in 4 kB pages
choices.why: No setting rewrites the data files into another page size; a different size needs a new cluster.

choices.text: Nothing: it is fixed at compile time
choices.why: Right. `block_size` is read-only; changing it means building PostgreSQL and a new cluster.

choices.text: full_page_writes is switched off automatically
choices.why: Nothing switches it off, and on ext4 it must stay on.

prompt: Which mount option should never be used under a PostgreSQL data directory?
hint: Which one makes fsync meaningless?

choices.text: barrier=0
choices.why: Right. Without barriers a flush may not reach stable storage, and a power cut can lose committed transactions.

choices.text: noatime
choices.why: noatime only stops access-time updates, which PostgreSQL never reads. It is safe.

choices.text: relatime
choices.why: relatime is the default and harmless; it updates access times at most once a day.

choices.text: defaults
choices.why: defaults gives the distribution's normal options, barriers included.

prompt: A team on Red Hat Enterprise Linux asks whether to reformat as ext4 because the course uses ext4. What does the lesson advise?
hint: Where should the attention go instead?

choices.text: Reformat: PostgreSQL is only supported on ext4
choices.why: PostgreSQL runs on both, and XFS is where many production servers live.

choices.text: Move to NFS, so the data is safe on another machine
choices.why: A network filesystem is the one the lesson says to avoid unless the vendor documents it for databases.

choices.text: Keep XFS, the distribution's default, and look at the disk
choices.why: Right. Both are well tested for PostgreSQL; the disk matters far more than the choice between them.

choices.text: Switch to tmpfs for speed
choices.why: tmpfs lives in memory and loses everything at a reboot.

prompt: A data filesystem listed in /etc/fstab fails to mount at boot, and the server starts PostgreSQL anyway. What has happened?
hint: What is at the mount point when nothing is mounted on it?

choices.text: PostgreSQL reads the data through the device name instead
choices.why: PostgreSQL only knows a directory path. It never opens the device.

choices.text: The kernel mounts it later, and PostgreSQL waits for the files to appear
choices.why: Nothing waits. What PostgreSQL finds at start is what it uses.

choices.text: It found an empty directory
choices.why: Right. The mount point is an ordinary empty directory until something is mounted on it, so the server has no data there.

choices.text: The data is read from the operating system's cache
choices.why: After a boot the cache is empty, and it never held a whole filesystem anyway.

prompt: Which row of `pg_test_fsync` tells you what your server's commits wait on, with the default settings?
hint: Linux's default wal_sync_method.

choices.text: Non-sync'ed 8kB writes
choices.why: That row never waits for the disk; it measures the kernel's memory.

choices.text: fdatasync
choices.why: Right. It is Linux's default wal_sync_method, so each commit waits about that long.

choices.text: fsync_writethrough
choices.why: It printed n/a: that method does not exist on Linux.

choices.text: 16 * 1kB open_sync writes
choices.why: That compares write sizes for open_sync, which the server does not use by default.

prompt: A cloud disk reports 900,000 fdatasync operations a second in pg_test_fsync. What should you conclude?
hint: Compare with the tmpfs run.

choices.text: It is fast
choices.why: Too fast to be a real flush. A disk that fast without a protected cache loses commits on a power cut.

choices.text: A flush is probably not reaching durable storage
choices.why: Right. That is the tmpfs number: a write cache answering before the data is safe. Find out whether it has power protection.

choices.text: Switch wal_sync_method to open_datasync
choices.why: The method is not the question. The number says the promise of a flush may not be kept at all.

choices.text: Commits will be limited by the processor
choices.why: The question is durability, not speed. A suspiciously fast flush is a risk, not a bottleneck.

prompt: On Ubuntu, pg_test_fsync is not on the PATH. It lives in /usr/lib/postgresql/16/___.
hint: Where every server program of version 16 lives.

prompt: `pg_wal` holds 337 MB and `max_wal_size` is 1GB. Which size is a reasonable floor for a dedicated pg_wal filesystem?
hint: max_wal_size is soft.

choices.text: 512 MB, comfortably above the 337 MB measured today
choices.why: Today's size is not the limit. This is the size the lesson made on purpose so it would fill.

choices.text: 1 GB, exactly max_wal_size
choices.why: The limit is where a checkpoint is asked for, not a ceiling; the log can pass it.

choices.text: 2 GB
choices.why: Right. Twice max_wal_size, because WAL keeps arriving while the checkpoint it triggered runs.

choices.text: 400 MB, the measured size plus a margin
choices.why: The log can grow to around max_wal_size between checkpoints, far past what it holds today.

prompt: Put the steps for moving pg_wal of an existing cluster to a new, mounted filesystem in order.
hint: The server must not be running while files move.
trap: Linking before moving fails, because pg_wal still exists as a directory.

prompt: On the course's virtual machine both filesystems are files on the same physical drive. What does separating pg_wal still buy there?
hint: The lesson gives two reasons; one needs separate devices.

choices.text: Faster commits, since the checkpoint no longer competes with them for the same disk
choices.why: On one physical drive they still compete. That benefit needs different devices.

choices.text: Each fills on its own, without the other
choices.why: Right. The space is separate even when the device is shared, so a full data filesystem does not stop the log, or the reverse.

choices.text: Smaller WAL files
choices.why: Segments stay 16 MB wherever they live.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: The space boundary is real on any machine; only the speed benefit is missing.

prompt: An INSERT into a table on a full tablespace fails with `could not extend file`. What happens to the server?
hint: Read the severity.

choices.text: It restarts every connection
choices.why: That is what a PANIC does, as when the log's filesystem fills. A data filesystem fails statements.

choices.text: It keeps running; only the statement failed
choices.why: Right. It is an ERROR: the statement is rolled back and every other query carries on.

choices.text: It shuts down until space is freed
choices.why: The server stays up; the next query read a million orders from the other disk.

choices.text: It becomes read-only
choices.why: PostgreSQL has no such mode for this. Writes elsewhere still work.

prompt: After the failed INSERT, `filler` has 0 rows. Why is its file still 51 MB?
hint: What does a rollback leave in the pages?

choices.text: Dead rows
choices.why: Right. The rolled-back rows stay in pages that exist until VACUUM removes them.

choices.text: The rows are still visible to other sessions
choices.why: count(*) returned 0. Nobody sees them; they only take space.

choices.text: ext4 does not report freed space until the filesystem is unmounted
choices.why: Nothing was freed. pg_relation_size reports the file itself, and it really is 51 MB.

choices.text: The write-ahead log keeps a copy inside the table
choices.why: The log lives in pg_wal, on another filesystem here.

prompt: `VACUUM filler` failed on the full filesystem, then succeeded after `tune2fs -m 0`. Why did that work for PostgreSQL?
hint: Who could use the reserved blocks before?

choices.text: tune2fs deleted the dead rows directly in the file
choices.why: tune2fs only changes filesystem settings; it knows nothing about rows.

choices.text: It grew the filesystem from 56 MB to 64 MB
choices.why: The size stayed 56M in df; only the reserved share changed.

choices.text: The root-only reserve became usable by postgres
choices.why: Right. ext4 keeps 5% for root; at 0% the postgres user got 3.2 MB, enough for the visibility map.

choices.text: It made VACUUM run as root
choices.why: The server always runs as postgres. The change was who may use the reserved blocks.

prompt: What does a PANIC mean for the sessions connected to the server?
hint: It is the severity above FATAL.

choices.text: Only the session that hit the error loses its connection
choices.why: That is FATAL. PANIC is one level above and takes every process with it.

choices.text: Only the current statement is rolled back
choices.why: That is ERROR, which is what a full tablespace gave.

choices.text: Every one of them is disconnected and the server restarts
choices.why: Right. A PANIC ends the whole server, not one statement or one session.

choices.text: Nothing, it is only written to the log
choices.why: The capture shows the client lost its connection and the cluster went down.

prompt: After the PANIC, the postmaster started crash recovery by itself. Why did the cluster still end up down?
hint: Read the line after `redo done`.

choices.text: Finishing recovery has to write WAL too
choices.why: Right. Recovery replayed to the end, then could not write a new log file on the full filesystem.

choices.text: The data files were corrupted by the crash and recovery refused to read them
choices.why: redo done means replay succeeded. Nothing was corrupted; there was no room to write.

choices.text: systemd does not restart PostgreSQL after a crash
choices.why: The postmaster did restart itself; recovery ran and failed for lack of space.

choices.text: max_wal_size forbids a restart
choices.why: No setting forbids it. The startup process failed on a write.

prompt: `walfill` was created with 1,000,000 rows, then the loop ran INSERTs of 1,000,000 rows each: three printed INSERT 0 1000000 and the fourth hit the PANIC. How many rows did `walfill` have after recovery?
hint: Only what committed survives.

prompt: With `vm.overcommit_memory = 2`, what happens when a backend asks for memory beyond the limit?
hint: Where does the failure land?

choices.text: Only that query fails, with an out of memory error
choices.why: Right. The request is refused inside the process that made it, and the rest of the server carries on.

choices.text: The OOM killer chooses the largest process
choices.why: That is the default, overcommit 0, which the setting exists to avoid.

choices.text: The postmaster restarts every connection to free memory for the backend that asked
choices.why: The restart follows a killed backend. With overcommit 2 nobody is killed.

choices.text: The kernel moves shared buffers to swap
choices.why: Nothing is moved; the allocation is simply refused.

prompt: A 4 GB server with no swap gets `vm.overcommit_memory = 2` and nothing else. What is the risk?
hint: Which other setting decides the limit?

choices.text: The OOM killer becomes more aggressive
choices.why: With 2 the kernel refuses allocations instead of killing; the problem is how low the limit is.

choices.text: The whole machine commits at most 2 GB
choices.why: Right. The limit is swap plus overcommit_ratio per cent of memory, and the default ratio is 50.

choices.text: Huge pages stop working
choices.why: The two settings are independent.

choices.text: None, because PostgreSQL is designed for it
choices.why: PostgreSQL recommends it, together with a ratio that leaves the server enough memory.

prompt: `huge_pages` is `try` and `HugePages_Total` is 0. What is the server using?
hint: What does try do when none are reserved?

choices.text: Ordinary pages, silently
choices.why: Right. try falls back without a word, which is why on is the honest value once pages are reserved.

choices.text: 72 huge pages it reserved for itself at start
choices.why: PostgreSQL cannot reserve them; the kernel has to, with vm.nr_hugepages.

choices.text: Nothing: it refuses to start
choices.why: That is huge_pages = on. The server in the capture was running.

choices.text: Transparent huge pages
choices.why: AnonHugePages and ShmemHugePages were 0 as well; shared buffers are not in huge pages at all.

prompt: Match each full filesystem to what PostgreSQL does.
hint: ERROR, PANIC, and a refusal to finish starting.

pairs.right: FATAL in the startup process, cluster down

prompt: At 3 a.m. pg_wal's filesystem is full and the cluster will not start. A colleague proposes deleting the ten oldest files in pg_wal. What do you do instead?
hint: The log is the only copy of changes not yet in the data files.

choices.text: Run pg_resetwal first, since it is the official tool for exactly this situation
choices.why: pg_resetwal throws the log away and can leave the database inconsistent. It is a last resort, not the first step.

choices.text: Give the filesystem room, then start
choices.why: Right. Grow it or free something else on it; recovery then replays and finishes with a checkpoint.

choices.text: Lower max_wal_size and restart
choices.why: Recycling needs a running server, and it cannot start.

choices.text: Delete them, but only the ones older than the last checkpoint
choices.why: You cannot tell from outside which are still needed, and recovery needs everything since the checkpoint it starts from.

prompt: A new storage array shows 2,000 fdatasync a second and the vendor says it has a battery-backed cache. A second array shows 600,000 and has no battery. Which one belongs under pg_wal?
hint: Speed is not the question; the promise is.

choices.text: The second, because commits will be three hundred times faster
choices.why: Fast until the power goes, and then committed transactions are lost with nothing in the log.

choices.text: Either, as long as full_page_writes stays on
choices.why: full_page_writes repairs torn pages; it cannot recover a commit the disk never stored.

choices.text: The first
choices.why: Right. Its number is plausible and its cache survives a power cut. The second is flushing to memory with nothing behind it.

choices.text: Neither: the WAL belongs on tmpfs
choices.why: tmpfs loses everything at a reboot. That is the worst place for the log.

prompt: Which of these return space to a full tablespace's filesystem? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which ones remove the file's pages rather than the rows' visibility?

choices.text: TRUNCATE on a disposable table
choices.why: Yes. The file goes when the transaction commits.

choices.text: DELETE FROM the largest table
choices.why: No. DELETE leaves dead rows in the same pages; the file keeps its size.

choices.text: ALTER TABLE ... SET TABLESPACE to one with room
choices.why: Yes, at the price of a lock while it copies.

choices.text: Growing the filesystem
choices.why: Yes, and it is the way that does not depend on what is in the tables.

choices.text: Deleting the largest numbered file by hand
choices.why: No. That file is a table, which then errors on every read.

prompt: The kernel reserves pages of 2 MB in advance when you set the sysctl vm.___ in /etc/sysctl.d.
hint: nr_ is how the kernel says number of.
